## EXAMPLE: exploratory plots and a shuffle comparison (delete this block)

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Tooth length by vitamin C dose and supplement type (n = 60)."

tooth <- ToothGrowth |>
  mutate(dose = factor(dose), supp = factor(supp, labels = c("Orange juice", "Ascorbic acid")))

ggplot(tooth, aes(x = dose, y = len, fill = supp)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length", fill = "Supplement")
```

*Interpretation:* Tooth length rises steadily with dose for both supplements.
At 0.5 and 1 mg/day, orange juice seems to give longer teeth than ascorbic acid,
but the boxes overlap at 2 mg/day. This motivates Hypothesis 2 (dose effect and
interaction) and Hypothesis 1 (supplement effect).

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-shuffle
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Real data (top left) compared with five copies in which tooth length was randomly shuffled."
#| fig-height: 5

# Shuffle the outcome within five copies of the data, then add the real data.
shuffled <- map(1:5, \(i) tooth |> mutate(len = sample(len), panel = paste("Shuffled", i))) |>
  list_rbind()
lineup <- bind_rows(tooth |> mutate(panel = "Real data"), shuffled) |>
  mutate(panel = fct_relevel(panel, "Real data"))

ggplot(lineup, aes(x = dose, y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length")
```

*Interpretation:* Only the real-data panel shows a clear upward trend with dose.
The shuffled panels look flat. This suggests the dose pattern is not just
random variation, so it is worth testing formally.
:::

## EXAMPLE: reporting results (delete this block)

**Hypothesis 1: Welch two-sample t-test.**

```{r}
#| label: example-h1

h1 <- t.test(len ~ supp, data = tooth)  # Welch: does not assume equal variances
h1
```

*Result:* The mean tooth length was `r round(h1$estimate[1], 1)` for orange juice
and `r round(h1$estimate[2], 1)` for ascorbic acid,
t(`r round(h1$parameter, 1)`) = `r round(h1$statistic, 2)`,
p = `r signif(h1$p.value, 2)`, 95% CI for the difference
[`r round(h1$conf.int[1], 2)`, `r round(h1$conf.int[2], 2)`].
Because p > 0.05 and the interval includes 0, we **fail to reject H~0~**.
Averaged over all doses, the data do not show a clear difference between the
supplements.

**Hypothesis 2: two-way ANOVA with interaction.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-h2
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Residual diagnostics for the two-way ANOVA."
#| fig-height: 4

h2 <- aov(len ~ dose * supp, data = tooth)
summary(h2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(h2, which = 1:2)  # residuals vs fitted (equal variance), Q-Q (normality)
```

*Result:* Dose, supplement and their interaction are all significant
(p < 0.05), so we **reject H~0~**. The residual plots show roughly constant
spread and approximately normal residuals, so the ANOVA assumptions are
reasonable. Notice that supplement type *is* significant once dose is taken
into account, even though the simple t-test in Hypothesis 1 was not. Controlling
for another variable can change a conclusion.
:::
